Ganymede. The largest moon in the solar system and the second-largest Galilean moon of Jupiter. Larger than the planet Mercury, Ganymede has a diverse geology featuring ancient impact basins, younger grooved terrain, and compelling evidence of a subsurface water ocean beneath its icy crust. It was discovered by Galileo Galilei in sixteen ten and is unique among moons in possessing its own magnetic field.

Ganymede has a diameter of five thousand two hundred sixty-eight kilometers, making it the largest moon in the solar system and larger than Mercury. Evidence suggests a liquid-water layer more than one hundred kilometers thick beneath an icy crust, containing more water than all of Earth's oceans combined. The moon generates its own magnetosphere, which is weak but measurable, unlike other moons. This makes Ganymede unique among the solar system's moons.

The surface shows distinctive grooved terrain, which is younger and lighter, and dark terrain, which is ancient and heavily cratered. The ice composition suggests a history of cryovolcanism, though Ganymede lacks the intense tidal heating of its neighboring moon Io. Ganymede was discovered by Galileo in sixteen ten as one of the four Galilean moons, making it historically significant as evidence for the heliocentric model. The moon is named after the Trojan prince who was abducted by Zeus in the form of an eagle. Ganymede's diverse geology and subsurface ocean make it a compelling world for understanding how planetary bodies evolve and sustain liquid water.
